From Knowledge to Practice: Analyzing Contraceptive Behavior Among Reproductive-Age Women in Malawi Using DHS Data

Rokaya AITLHAJ-MHAND

2025-07-04

INTRODUCTION

Despite global advancements in reproductive health, many low- and middle-income countries continue to face significant challenges in family planning uptake and utilization. Sub-Saharan Africa, in particular, reports persistently high fertility rates and low contraceptive prevalence, contributing to unintended pregnancies, maternal morbidity, and socio-economic instability. Malawi, a landlocked country in southeastern Africa, exemplifies this trend, with a notable gap between knowledge of contraception and its actual use among women of reproductive age (15–49 years). According to the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), awareness of modern contraceptive methods in Malawi is nearly universal. However, the translation of this knowledge into consistent and effective contraceptive practice remains uneven across different population groups. Factors such as age, education, marital status, place of residence, religion, and economic status play crucial roles in shaping individual decisions about contraceptive use. Understanding these dynamics is essential for tailoring public health interventions that address both informational and structural barriers to contraceptive access and use.

Aim This study aims to examine how contraceptive knowledge translates into contraceptive practice among reproductive-age women (15–49 years) in Malawi. Specifically, it seeks to analyze how sociodemographic factors influence the gap between knowledge and actual use of contraception.

Overview of Demographic and Socioeconomic Characteristics of Women in Malawi

Table 1 presents the distribution of key demographic and socioeconomic characteristics among 24,562 women of reproductive age in Malawi. The age groups are fairly evenly distributed, with the largest proportions in the youngest brackets: 15–19 years (21.5%) and 20–24 years (20.7%). Geographically, the majority of participants reside in the southern region (46.2%), followed by the central (34.3%) and northern regions (19.6%).

Religious affiliation is predominantly Christian, with 42.3% identifying as “other Christian,” 17.6% Catholic, and 15.8% CCAP. Muslims make up 11.1%, while other religions and those reporting no religion represent a small minority.

Regarding marital status, most women are currently married or living with a partner (64.9%), while 21.7% have never been in union, and 13.4% are formerly in union. Literacy levels show that nearly two-thirds (64.9%) can read a whole sentence, but approximately 26% cannot read at all or have limited reading ability.

Education levels reveal that most women have attained primary education (61.2%), with smaller proportions having no education (11.3%), secondary education (24.7%), or higher education (2.8%).

The wealth index is relatively balanced across quintiles, though the richest group represents the largest segment (26.3%), and the poorest accounts for 17.4%.

Overall, this table highlights a predominantly young, married, and Christian population with varied educational attainment and socioeconomic status, reflecting the diverse profiles relevant for reproductive health and contraceptive use analyses in Malawi.

Age distribution by contraceptive use status

The box plot illustrates the age distribution of individuals currently using contraceptives. The median age of users is approximately 26 years, with the majority falling between 20 and 35 years old. This suggests that contraceptive use is most common among women in their reproductive prime. A smaller number of users are also observed below 20 and above 40 years of age, indicating that contraceptive use spans a broad age range, though it is less frequent at the extremes (Figure 1).

Contraceptive Use by Education Level

The bar chart illustrates the distribution of contraceptive use among women in Malawi by education level. The variable displayed is the percentage of women currently using contraception.Among the women who reported using contraceptive methods, the majority had attained primary education (61.2%), followed by those with secondary education (24.7%). A smaller proportion of users had no formal education (11.3%), while only 2.8% had attained a higher (post-secondary) education.

This distribution suggests that contraceptive use is most common among women with some level of formal education, particularly at the primary level, and highlights a positive association between education and contraceptive practice. However, the relatively low proportion of users with higher education may reflect broader educational access limitations or demographic trends in the population (Figure 2).

### Contraceptive Method by Education levels

The Barplot shows that Across all education levels, “not using” a contraceptive method remains the most common response, ranging from 52% to 61%. Among users, the most frequently reported method is injectable contraception, especially among women with primary education (24.4%) and no education (20.7%).

Use of implants and female sterilization follows, while methods like IUD, pill, and man condom are less common but more frequent among women with higher education. Traditional methods (e.g., withdrawal, periodic abstinence, SDM) and LAM are minimally used across all groups.

This suggests that method mix varies by educational level, with more method diversity and slightly higher use of modern short-acting and barrier methods among more educated women (Figure 3).

Contraceptive Use by wealth index group

The barplot shows that The analysis of contraceptive use by wealth index group in Malawi reveals that a significant proportion of women across all socioeconomic strata are not using any contraceptive method, with non-use rates ranging from 51.6% among the poorer group to 56.7% among the richest. Modern contraceptive methods are the most commonly used among those practicing contraception, accounting for approximately 42% to 48% across all groups. Interestingly, modern method use does not increase steadily with wealth; in fact, usage is slightly higher among the poorer and middle groups than among the richest. Traditional and folkloric methods remain marginal, with usage rates below 1% in all quintiles. These findings suggest that while economic status plays a role, it may not be the sole determinant of contraceptive behavior, highlighting the importance of considering additional factors such as education, accessibility, cultural beliefs, and healthcare outreach (Figure 4).

contraceptive methode by place residence

Among women in Malawi, contraceptive use differs slightly between urban and rural areas. In urban areas, 42.6% of women use modern contraceptive methods, while 56.5% do not use any method. Traditional and folkloric methods are used by less than 1% each.

In rural areas, the percentage of women using modern methods is somewhat lower at 45.3%, but the proportion of women not using any method is also slightly lower at 53.9%. Traditional and folkloric methods remain rare, used by less than 1% of women.

Overall, urban women show marginally higher uptake of modern contraceptive methods compared to rural women, but non-use remains the largest group in both settings (Figure 5)

Conclusion

This study, set out to explore how widespread awareness of contraception translates into actual use among women aged 15–49. Despite near-universal knowledge of modern contraceptive methods in Malawi, the findings reveal a significant gap between knowledge and practice. While many women are aware of contraceptive options, a large proportion still do not use them, highlighting barriers beyond simple awareness.

The analysis showed that contraceptive use is most common among younger women, especially those in their twenties, and declines with age. Educational attainment strongly influences use: women with primary and secondary education are more likely to use contraception, while usage is lower among those with no education or limited access to higher education. Interestingly, contraceptive use does not consistently increase with wealth, suggesting that socioeconomic status alone does not predict behavior. Similarly, while urban women use modern methods slightly more than rural women, non-use remains high in both settings.

These patterns emphasize that moving from knowledge to practice requires more than information dissemination. Structural, cultural, and accessibility-related barriers must be addressed. Tailored public health strategies that consider age, education, place of residence, and economic status are essential for closing the gap between contraceptive awareness and effective use, ultimately advancing reproductive health equity for women in Malawi.
